node.label: Jacquelyn Dowd Hall
node.date_label: Revolt Against Chivalry (1979) · Like a Family, coauthored (1987) · “The Long Civil Rights Movement” (2005) · Sisters and Rebels (2019)
node.description: In “The Long Civil Rights Movement and the Political Uses of the Past” (2005), Hall argues that the struggle extended beyond the familiar 1954–1965 southern campaign and joined racial equality to economic justice. She challenges public narratives that celebrate civil-rights victories while obscuring these wider demands. Earlier, Like a Family: The Making of a Southern Cotton Mill World (1987), written with five co-authors from Southern Oral History Program research, presented Piedmont mill workers’ culture and politics as a history of resistance and radicalism. Stephanie McCurry’s 1992 review essay judged its neglect of racial conflict the book’s greatest weakness. Sundiata Keita Cha-Jua and Clarence Lang’s “The ‘Long Movement’ as Vampire” (2007) criticized the Long Movement thesis for exaggerating continuity in African American social movements and for collapsing the concepts of Civil Rights and Black Power. Revolt Against Chivalry (1979; revised 1993) links women’s antilynching activism to struggles over racial justice and women’s authority. Hall also founded and directed UNC’s Southern Oral History Program.

node.scope_note: The 2005 article was read only in the licensed OUP excerpt; its argument is otherwise characterised through secondary accounts (JSTOR Daily, a university lecture record). An interview excerpt and institutional and publisher accounts were read; the 2007 critique was not read on a permitted route. Monographs, Dudziak’s book, Kelley’s foreword, the complete Berlin review, oral-history collections and linked audio remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As founding director of UNC's Southern Oral History Program, Hall built a programme to document the lives of ordinary people and insisted that it be fully integrated into the history department.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: OHA report, paragraphs beginning When Jacquelyn and Telling the stories, lines 90–92; UNC Press Description and author credits, lines 34–38 and 70–76. These are substantive institutional and publisher accounts; no interview corpus or full monograph was read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Revolt Against Chivalry (1979; revised 1993) connects white southern women’s antilynching activism with struggles over women’s authority and racial justice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Columbia publisher description, lines 62–65, especially its account of Ames linking opposition to violence with self-definition. Oxford biography supplies original 1979; Columbia dates the revised edition to 1993. Description only; the book is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Like a Family (1987), written collaboratively by Hall and five co-authors from Southern Oral History Program interviews, presents the culture and politics of Piedmont cotton-mill workers as a history of resistance and radicalism, as Stephanie McCurry’s 1992 review essay characterizes it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UNC Press Description and Praise, lines 70–87; all six author credits, line 36. Read publisher account and attributed review excerpts only, not the book. This is a contribution to labour history, not a claim based solely on Hall’s professional office.

proposed_edges.relationship: “The Long Civil Rights Movement” (2005) examines how public remembrance narrows the struggle’s chronology and economic goals.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed Oxford excerpt, lines 10–15, including “remembrance is always a form of forgetting”; primary pp. 1233–1235. Read the licensed passage and selected original pages; no museum or commemoration corpus independently examined.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Long Civil Rights Movement and the Political Uses of the Past” (2005), Hall traces the civil rights struggle back to the “liberal and radical milieu of the late 1930s” and carries it beyond the landmark legislation of the 1960s into the 1970s, as JSTOR Daily (2024) and the University of Mississippi’s 2014 Gilder-Jordan lecture record summarize it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: (1) JSTOR Daily, Matthew Wills, “The Long Civil Rights Movement” (8 Sept. 2024, updated 3 Dec. 2025), opening paragraph: Hall’s “influential exploration of the ‘long civil rights movement’ that began not in the mid-1950s but earlier, in the ‘liberal and radical milieu of the late 1930s’”; later: “Hall describes six major threads braiding together during the long civil rights movement”. (2) eGrove (University of Mississippi) record of the 2014 Gilder-Jordan Lecture: Hall “advanced an understanding of a dynamic movement not bound by 1954’s Brown v. Board and the Civil Rights Act of 1965”. Distinct from jdh_w_09 (memory), which concerns how public remembrance narrows the struggle. This edge concerns the movement’s chronology and the field’s framework. Target ‘black’ is the closest existing field node; there is no separate civil-rights historiography node. The Cha-Jua and Lang critique (2007) remains the main reception; its authors have no endpoints.
proposed_edges.map_label: The long civil rights movement framework

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Later Comment” (Journal of American History, 1997), her response to Joel Williamson’s “Wounds Not Scars”, Hall takes up Benedict Anderson’s argument, from the revised Imagined Communities (1991), that the modern nation-state depends on an oscillation between remembering and forgetting. She uses it to suggest that lynching has not been forgotten but is one of the evils “we are doomed both to remember and to forget.”
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read on the publisher’s own landing page for JAH 83:4 (March 1997), 1268–1272, Round Table “What We See and Can’t See in the Past”. Oxford Academic shows a first-page preview image of p. 1268 there, and I read the whole of that page. In the second paragraph, beginning “The symbiosis between cultural amnesia and historiographical neglect is not, of course, unique to the American South”, Hall writes: “Benedict Anderson has argued that the modern nation-state depends on the oscillation between remembering and forgetting. But atrocities banished from official memory are not in fact forgotten; rather, he says, conflicting memories are buried near the surface of consciousness ... memories we are supposed to forget.” Note 1 cites Anderson, Imagined Communities (London, 1991), 187–206, the chapter added to the 1991 edition; the book first appeared in 1983. She continues: “Lynching, I would suggest, has not been forgotten ... But it is perhaps one of those evils that we are doomed both to remember and to forget.” Anderson’s argument is in the body text and frames her own claim, so this is not a citation-only use. It follows the graph’s precedent for using Anderson’s framework (edge_2078, Anderson -> Ngai; edge_2796, Anderson -> Higginbotham). An editorial footnote on p. 1268 says Hall wrote the comment after the Journal accepted Williamson’s article and with access to the referees’ reports. Pp. 1269–1272 are unread, including whatever she says about the referees, among them Robin D. G. Kelley. No claim is made about Anderson’s influence on Hall’s other work.
proposed_edges.map_label: Anderson’s remembering and forgetting applied to lynching

proposed_edges.relationship: In Haunted by Empire (2006), Ann Laura Stoler uses Hall’s account of lynching and white chivalry to compare imperial racial logics and acknowledges conceptual borrowing from Hall’s work in ‘Tense and Tender Ties’ (2001; reprinted 2006).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the relevant preface and chapter passages in the licensed Duke University Press book preview. The preface places Hall’s account of lynching and white chivalry alongside colonial racial and sexual anxieties in Stoler’s discussion of her comparative research. On p. 31 Stoler includes herself through the first-person plural in an account of colonial scholars drawing on Hall, then qualifies this borrowing as often privileging conceptual form over historical content. This is substantive discussion in the body, not a collective bibliographic note. The copyright page identifies the chapter’s original publication in the Journal of American History in December 2001. The preview does not include the chapter’s endnotes or the complete volume; no particular Hall title or additional debt is inferred from unread notes.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall’s racial-violence analysis informs Stoler’s comparisons

proposed_edges.relationship: Dianne Feeley’s review ‘Northern Freedom Chronicles’ (2013) identifies Hall’s long civil rights movement conception as an inspiration for Thomas J. Sugrue’s Sweet Land of Liberty (2008), his history of northern African American struggles for equality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Feeley’s review on Against the Current’s own site, issue 162, January/February 2013. The opening discussion explicitly attributes Sugrue’s northern synthesis to inspiration from Hall’s conception, rather than merely listing scholars with a shared topic. The relationship is deliberately attributed to Feeley’s review. Sugrue’s complete introduction and book were not read; the publisher’s text sample and the available introduction preview pages did not expose the relevant acknowledgment. The review’s bibliographic heading and the publisher’s ebook listing establish the book’s original 2008 publication. This is an influence reported by a reviewer, not a claim to have read Sugrue’s own statement of debt and not a review edge between Feeley and Hall.
proposed_edges.map_label: Long-movement framework informs Sugrue’s northern history
